q: How does the concentration of the measurement distribution on |-s mod p> scale precisely as p grows through primes p == 1 vs 3 (mod 4)? Our exact simulations at p in {13, 31, 61} give P(correct) = 1 - 1/p almost exactly; is the correction term identical across the two Gauss-sum sign classes, or does the +/-i Gauss-sum phase change the sub-leading error scaling in ways the paper's proof suppresses under the O(1) probability bound?
basis: Our numeric results give min P(correct) exactly (p-1)/p for all three primes (13, 31, 61 — spanning both residue classes mod 4), matching to 6 decimals. But the paper only proves 'exponentially close to 1' as an asymptotic bound, not the exact functional form 1 - 1/p we observed. Whether that exact tight bound holds asymptotically is a concrete testable follow-up.
next_steps: Run the same exact-QFT simulation on all primes up to (say) p = 500; fit the deviation delta_p = 1 - P(correct); check whether delta_p exactly equals 1/p or has residue-class-dependent higher-order terms (e.g., 1/p + c/p^{3/2} with c distinct for p == 1 vs 3 mod 4).

q: What is the *unconditional* classical query lower bound for SLSP identification, independent of Damgard-style pseudo-randomness conjectures? Existing arguments either give a trivial Omega(log p) (info-theoretic) or Omega(p) (marginal-bias) or Omega(p^2) (two-point correlation) — but no proof of Omega(sqrt p) or better unconditionally.
basis: Our lower-bound experiment (c) shows two-point correlations are all -1/p (Jacobsthal identity), so a correlation-attack SNR bound gives Omega(p^2) queries — but this ignores adaptive strategies. The paper punts on this by citing Damgard's conjecture. We measured this three ways and got three different scalings, exposing the absence of a tight unconditional bound.
next_steps: Try to prove an information-theoretic Omega(sqrt p) bound via the standard polynomial-method technique applied to the SLSP acceptance polynomial, or refute it by exhibiting a subquadratic classical algorithm using higher-order character-sum estimates (Weil, Deligne).

q: Does the 2-query quantum speedup survive when the oracle f_s(x) has independent noise on each query (bit-flip probability eta)? The paper implicitly assumes a perfect oracle; but real quantum implementations would face oracle noise, and the algorithm's success depends on cancellation of Gauss-sum phases that could be very sensitive.
basis: Our simulation is noiseless. The 1/p error floor we observe comes purely from the discreteness of F_p; oracle noise would inject arbitrary +/-1 flips into a linear combination that the QFT then coherently mixes, potentially destroying the concentration on |-s>. This is not discussed in the paper.
next_steps: Add a per-query bit-flip channel (eta = 0.01, 0.05, 0.1) to the oracle in Step 1 and Step 3 of shifted_legendre_algo.py, measure P(correct) as a function of (p, eta), and check whether the algorithm degrades gracefully (~ 1 - c*eta) or catastrophically (~ 1 - c*eta*p). If the latter, quantum error correction would be required even at the algorithmic level.

q: How well does the algorithm work when the exact QFT is replaced by the Hales-Hallgren epsilon-approximate QFT that the paper actually assumes exists for prime p? The paper cites [Hales-Hallgren FOCS 2000] as if that approximate QFT is drop-in, but the actual approximation quality needed to preserve the 1 - 1/p tightness is not analysed.
basis: We used the exact p-dimensional DFT matrix (numerically exact to double-precision roundoff). The paper's actual assumed QFT is an O((log p)^2)-gate approximation with additive error epsilon. It's unclear whether that epsilon needs to shrink as O(1/p) (giving overhead poly(log p) * log p) or O(1/sqrt p) or O(1). The precise threshold governs the paper's stated 'polynomial time' claim.
next_steps: Implement the Hales-Hallgren approximate QFT (or a Kitaev-style variant) and re-run Algorithm 1 at p in {13, 31, 61, 127, 251} with epsilon in {1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4}, measuring P(correct) vs epsilon. Extract the empirical scaling epsilon* = epsilon_max(p) for which P(correct) >= 1 - 1/p / 2.

q: Does the same 2-query algorithmic pattern (uniform superposition -> Fourier sample -> multiplicative character -> inverse Fourier) extend to higher-degree residues, e.g., recovering s from an oracle f_s(x) = ((x+s)/p)_k for the k-th power residue symbol (which is a character of order k, not order 2)? The paper is entirely about the quadratic case; the trace-based Fourier machinery in Section 5 hints at generality but never spells out the k-th-residue variant.
basis: Our simulation shows the algorithm is exact for the quadratic (order-2) character. The essential ingredient — a Gauss-sum evaluation — has known generalisations for higher-order characters (all with magnitude sqrt(p)). It's not obvious whether the paper's Step 3 'multiply by character' cancels the y-dependent phase for k-th-power characters or leaves a residual y-dependence that spoils the inverse-QFT concentration.
next_steps: Implement a cubic-residue oracle f_s(x) = ((x+s)/p)_3 for primes p == 1 mod 3 (e.g., p = 7, 13, 19, 31) and try the analogous 3-step algorithm using cubic Gauss sums. Measure whether s is recoverable from |−s> or from a coset thereof. If yes, this is an immediate extension of the paper's result; if not, characterise what the correct multi-step algorithm looks like.
